original_question: Is there a quantum algorithm for the search conjugacy problem in a polycyclic group that lowers the complexity of solving that problem?
target_in_paper: Section 11, "Open Problems," under "Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Complexity," item 1: "Is there any quantum algorithm for solving the search conjugacy problem for polycyclic group that reduces the complexity of the algorithm?" This is the nearest official formulation to your draft. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper’s core target almost exactly: it asks about a quantum algorithm, it focuses on the search conjugacy problem, it restricts attention to polycyclic groups, and it asks whether the complexity can be reduced. It is therefore very close to the paper’s own open-problem wording. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
missing_details: The paper states the problem for polycyclic groups as a class, not for one specific fixed polycyclic group. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

To be fully stand-alone, the question should define the search conjugacy problem itself: given conjugate elements a,b in a group G, find an element x in G such that b = x^{-1}ax. The paper uses exactly this search task in its cryptographic discussion of the Kahrobaei–Khan ElGamal-type protocol. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The nearby computational model is not arbitrary: Section 8 treats polycyclic groups via consistent polycyclic presentations, where elements have unique normal forms and computation proceeds through those normal forms. That representation-theoretic context is implicit in the open problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Section 8 says that the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups is solvable, but that its complexity is unknown and widely conjectured to be exponential time. So a faithful rewrite should ask for a quantum improvement over the known/classical complexity landscape, without hard-coding a stronger claim such as a proven exponential classical bound. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The immediately preceding quantum-context sentence discusses quantum algorithms for polycyclic groups in both finite and infinite settings; that ambient scope is part of the nearby context, even though the specific item is phrased more tersely. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The paper does not specify worst-case, average-case, or generic-case complexity in this quantum item. Those complexity notions are separated elsewhere in Section 11, so a paper-faithful rewrite should not insert one of them unless explicitly stated. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
refined_question: Let G be a polycyclic group represented by a consistent polycyclic presentation, so that elements admit unique normal forms. Given conjugate elements a,b in G, is there a quantum algorithm for the search conjugacy problem—i.e., for finding x in G such that b = x^{-1}ax—that reduces the computational complexity of solving this problem compared with the corresponding classical algorithms for polycyclic groups used in cryptography? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
justification: The draft clearly points to the explicit open problem in Section 11 rather than to any theorem or proposition elsewhere in the paper. To make that question mathematically self-contained without broadening it, one has to import only the nearby context the paper itself supplies: Section 8 explains the polycyclic-group computational setting through consistent polycyclic presentations and normal forms, and it records that the search conjugacy problem is solvable in polycyclic groups while its complexity remains unknown and is widely conjectured exponential. Section 4 gives the operative search-conjugacy task used in the paper’s cryptographic protocols. That is why the refined version keeps the target narrow—quantum improvement for the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups—rather than drifting to broader questions about quantum algorithms for group-based cryptography in general. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
